reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: The conus medullaris is the tapered caudal end of the cord, lying at about the first lumbar vertebral level in adults, and contains the sacral segments that govern bladder, bowel and sexual reflex arcs
A lesion here causes early and severe sphincter disturbance, with urinary retention and overflow incontinence, faecal incontinence and erectile dysfunction, often out of proportion to limb weakness
Sensory loss is typically symmetrical and confined to the saddle region, and pain tends to be less prominent than in cauda equina syndrome
Because it is the junction of cord and roots, the syndrome can combine upper and lower motor neurone signs, so ankle reflexes may be lost while other reflexes are variably preserved
The distinction from cauda equina syndrome matters, as the latter is more asymmetrical, more painful and radicular, with purely lower motor neurone features and later bladder involvement
Epiconus lesions just above the conus cause more pronounced lower limb weakness with relatively preserved sphincter function
Common causes include central disc prolapse, intramedullary and extramedullary tumours, trauma and cord ischaemia
Acute retention with saddle anaesthesia is a neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent imaging and decompression
reference.pathophysiology: The conus medullaris houses the second to fifth sacral cord segments, which contain the parasympathetic and somatic centres controlling micturition, defaecation and sexual reflexes, together with the sacral dermatomal representation of the saddle area. A lesion of the conus damages these segmental reflex centres directly, producing early autonomic failure and symmetrical saddle sensory loss. Because the conus is also the site where the lower lumbar and sacral nerve roots begin to exit, a lesion here can additionally injure these roots, generating a mixture of upper motor neurone signs from cord damage and lower motor neurone signs from root involvement; the anatomical compactness of the sacral segments explains why relatively small lesions cause disproportionately severe sphincter and saddle deficits.
additionalDifferentials: Conus tumour such as ependymoma or metastasis
Transverse myelitis affecting the lower cord
additionalInvestigations: Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine with contrast to identify a compressive or intrinsic lesion
Bladder ultrasound or catheterisation to measure post-void residual volume
Urodynamic studies to characterise the pattern of bladder dysfunction
Digital rectal examination to assess anal tone and voluntary contraction
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis where an inflammatory or neoplastic process is suspected
Oncological work-up and tumour markers when a mass lesion is identified
redFlags: Acute urinary retention with saddle anaesthesia, which constitutes a surgical emergency
Rapidly progressive lower limb or sphincter deficit
Loss of anal tone or absent bulbocavernosus reflex
Bilateral leg symptoms with a sensory level suggesting cord involvement
reference.prognosis: Bladder, bowel and sexual function often recover incompletely once deficits are established, and sphincter recovery tends to lag behind motor recovery. Early recognition and prompt decompression of a compressive cause offer the best chance of preserving function.
pitfalls: Confusing the syndrome with cauda equina compression and delaying urgent imaging
Performing an incomplete examination that omits saddle sensation and anal tone
Attributing urinary retention to a primary urological cause and missing the neurological lesion
Interpreting overflow incontinence as preserved or normal voiding
Failing to appreciate the mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs and thus mislocating the lesion
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Treat the underlying cause urgently: emergency surgical decompression of a compressive lesion offers the best chance of preserving sphincter and neurological function
Direct lesion-specific therapy where relevant, such as corticosteroids and radiotherapy or chemotherapy for a neoplastic or inflammatory cause
Manage neurogenic bladder with intermittent catheterisation for retention and overflow, with urodynamic-guided bladder care
Institute a structured bowel regimen with stimulant laxatives, suppositories and planned evacuation for faecal incontinence
Address erectile and sexual dysfunction with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and specialist input
Commence early neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy and occupational therapy, and monitor for pressure injury and recurrent urinary tract infection
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across neurosurgery, urology, continence and rehabilitation services
